title: The purse that must change
description: Keep the hero's coins right by handing values in and back, instead of reaching outside a function.

tasks.title: Names inside a function stay inside
tasks.body:
A name given a value inside a function is local: it exists only while that call runs, and a name outside with the same spelling is a different name.

A function can read a name from outside, but assigning to it inside makes a new local name.
tasks.detail:
So score = score + 1 inside a function stops with an UnboundLocalError: the function's own score has no value yet.

The clean fix is to hand the value in and return the new one: score = add_point(score). A global line would work too, but it makes a function harder to test and reuse.

tasks.code:
# Who changes the score?
score = 0

def bonus():
    score = 50
    print(score)

def add_point(points):
    return points + 1

bonus()
print(score)
score = add_point(score)
print(score)
tasks.note: bonus() makes its own local score, which disappears when the call ends, so the outer score is still 0. add_point() is handed the score and gives back a new value, which the caller stores.

tasks.question: What would happen if bonus() said score = score + 50 instead?
options: It prints 50, and the outer score stays 0
tasks.why: Because bonus() assigns to score, every score inside it is local, and the local one has no value yet when score + 50 is worked out.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: inside bonus(), add print(score) above the assignment, and read the error. Then call add_point() three times in a row, storing the result each time.

Write two functions for the hero's coins.

1. collect(coins, found) returns the hero's new number of coins after finding some more.
2. spend(coins, price) returns two values: the coins left and True if there were enough to pay, or the coins unchanged and False if there were not.

Neither function may change or depend on a name outside itself: hand the values in and return the answers. Your program should not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
tasks.starter: # Define collect(coins, found) and spend(coins, price)
hints: Everything each function needs arrives as a parameter, and everything it works out leaves by return. No name outside the functions is needed at all.
spend() has two outcomes: an if decides whether the coins cover the price, and each branch returns two values separated by a comma.
The same shape with other names: def eat(food, bite): return food - bite hands the new amount back, and the caller stores it with food = eat(food, 2).

error_hints.text: A function that assigns to coins makes its own local coins. Use the parameter instead, and return the new value.
Inside each function, use the parameters from its def line, spelled the same way.
collect(10, 5) should return 15: the coins handed in, plus the coins found.
spend(20, 8) should return 12 and True together.
When the price is more than the coins, nothing is paid: return the coins unchanged, and False.
Check spending every coin: having exactly the price is enough to pay.
Check an empty purse: the answer must come from the coins handed in, not from a name outside the function.

similar_example.code:
def eat(food, bite):
    return food - bite

food = 10
food = eat(food, 2)
food = eat(food, 3)
print(food)
similar_example.note: The amount goes in, a new amount comes back, and the caller stores it. Your spend() also says whether it could pay.

other_ways.note: Checking the refusal first means the normal case needs no else.

other_ways.code:
def collect(coins, found):
    total = coins
    total += found
    return total

def spend(coins, price):
    enough = coins >= price
    left = coins - price if enough else coins
    return left, enough
other_ways.note: Names made inside a function, like total and enough, are local: they cannot clash with anything outside.
